ads.title: The emergency contact
primary: I built a company to thirty million dollars a year and I was still the first number anyone called on a Sunday.
That is not ownership. That is a job with worse hours.
Nothing was wrong with my effort. I just could not see which part of my own business was holding it back, and working harder was never going to show me.
What I eventually found is in the book. Twenty-one dollars, and you have a hundred days to ask for your money back.
ads.headline: The Million Dollar Hurdle

ads.title: Somebody else's business
primary: Just get more leads. Hire someone. Work on the business, not in it. Put more into marketing. Get systems in place.
Every one of those is the right answer for somebody. All true, all useless until you know which one is actually yours, and picking wrong is how the last three years went.

There is a scorecard in the back of my book. Five sections, about ten minutes, and it names the one that is holding the other four down. Then you read those chapters first and leave the rest for later.
Twenty-one dollars. Hundred day guarantee.
ads.headline: All good advice. One of them is yours.
ads.description: Find out which in ten minutes.

ads.title: Nobody buys a business that needs you
ads.creative: Kitchen counter, book with phone and keys
primary: Here is the part nobody says out loud at the networking breakfast.
If you do everything in your business, you are the business. And nobody buys a business that cannot run without the owner in the middle of it.
That is not a growth problem. That is being locked in for life.
I spent twenty years building a company I could actually sell, and I got most of the lessons the expensive way. They are in the book, for twenty-one dollars.
ads.headline: Nobody buys a business that needs you.

ads.title: The post office job
primary: I grew up in a Boston housing project where the highest ambition anyone had was a steady job at the post office.

Four companies later, one of them went from me on my own to twenty five thousand customers and thirty million dollars a year. None of that came from being smarter than the owners I sit with now. It came from finding the one thing capping the business and fixing that before anything else. Every time.
That is what the book is. It is a USA Today bestseller and it hit number one on Amazon, which still feels strange to type.
Twenty-one dollars, and a hundred days to ask for your money back.
ads.headline: Housing project to $30M a year.

ads.title: They arrived
primary: Twelve years on the Inc. 5000 list and I still got a bit giddy opening this box.

The Million Dollar Hurdle is a USA Today bestseller and hit number one on Amazon. It is a book for the hands-on, self-made owner stuck under a million. The landscaper, the contractor, the dentist, the agency owner. The one who built something real and cannot work out why it will not go further.

There is a scorecard in the back. Five sections, about ten minutes, and it tells you which one is holding the other four down. That is the whole idea. Fix the one that is capping the rest, in that order, instead of guessing.
Twenty-one dollars, and a hundred days to ask for your money back.
ads.headline: USA Today bestseller. $21.

ads.title: The number nobody measures
primary: There is a number in most small businesses that nobody measures and it quietly decides who wins the deal.
It is how long it takes to call a new lead back. Inside one minute, acquisition goes up 391 percent. At two minutes it is 160. At an hour, 36.
Not a bigger ad budget. Not a better website. The gap between the form hitting the inbox and somebody picking up the phone.
That is one section of five in the book, and the scorecard in the back tells you whether it is the section that is costing you. Twenty-one dollars.
ads.headline: 391 percent. Nobody measures it.

ads.title: Which chapters were written for you
primary: Most business books have to assume your pipeline is fine, your hiring is fine and your pricing is fine, so they hand you a little of everything.
That is why you finish them agreeing with every word and changing nothing.
Mine opens with a scorecard instead. Five sections, about ten minutes, and it names the weakest one. That tells you which chapters were written for you and which can wait until next year.
Twenty-one dollars. The audiobook is free with the paperback.
ads.headline: Ten minutes to find your weak spot.

ads.title: Underlined, then forgotten
ads.creative: Book on the shelf among other business books
primary: There is a stack of business books beside my bed with underlining in the first forty pages and nothing after that.

I did not stop reading them because they were wrong. I stopped because none of them were about my business in particular, so I never knew which page to act on first. Agreeing with a book is not the same as using it.
That is the entire reason this one has a diagnostic in it instead of a summary chapter.
Twenty-one dollars, and a hundred days to send it back.
ads.headline: Underlined, then forgotten.
ads.description: This one tells you where to start.

ads.title: Technically on the course
primary: You know the guy. Technically on a golf course. Spiritually in a conference room. His playing partners know more about his Q3 than his wife does.
I was him for about ten years. That is not dedication. That is a business that cannot make a decision without you standing in the room.
The fix is not a longer list. It is finding the one part of the business that is capping all the others, and doing that part first.
Twenty-one dollars. Hundred day guarantee.
ads.headline: Technically on the course.

ads.title: Eight years
ads.creative: Book face down beside the legal pad
primary: "I can't find anyone who cares as much as I do."
I heard that from business owners for twenty years. I said it myself once.

At Taradel our average employee tenure was eight years, in an industry where that is close to unheard of. It was not luck and it was not pay. It was a three interview process where anyone in the room could veto a hire for any reason, including one they could not explain.
The whole process is in the book. Twenty-one dollars.
ads.headline: Eight year average tenure.
ads.description: The hiring process that did it.
